messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Housekeeper
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was nine years old when his stepfather's belt came off. He remembers the sound first—the leather sliding through the loops with a whisper that still lives in his nervous system—and then the weight of it, the particular roughness of that worn fabric against his skin as the man swung it in the dark hallway outside his bedroom. Marcus had woken to shouting, to the smell of alcohol, to the certainty that he had done something wrong, though he could never quite remember what. The blows came in a rhythm that felt endless. His stepfather's voice rose and fell like a tide. When it was over, Marcus lay on the cold floor in the dark, his body trembling, the texture of that belt still burning against his ribs and thighs. The darkness had become a weapon.

Now, at twenty-five, Marcus works as a housekeeper at a mid-sized hotel in Portland, a job that keeps him moving through other people's spaces during daylight hours. He is reliably competent—his supervisor notes he is thorough, if quiet—but something has shifted in recent months that no one quite names. When Marcus clocks out at five o'clock, the anxiety begins to climb. Nighttime feels like a trap closing. The dark of evening, the dark of his apartment, the dark of anywhere indoors once the sun sets, triggers a cascade that he has learned to recognize but cannot quite stop. The moment darkness falls, his body floods with the same dread it knew at nine: the sense that something terrible is about to happen, that he is unsafe, that the walls themselves have become dangerous. This is why he has started staying awake into the early morning hours, why he sits in the brightness of diners or twenty-four-hour laundromats, why he has called in sick to shifts that would require him to work the evening turnover. The avoidance has become automatic. When dusk approaches, Marcus simply cannot bring himself to go home.

But staying awake has its own cost. The exhaustion hollows him out, and in that hollow space, the memories return with a vividness that terrifies him. When he closes his eyes—even for a moment—the film plays: the hallway, the sound, the belt, the taste of fear in his mouth. It feels completely real, as though it is happening again, his body seized by the same panic it knew two decades ago. The memory comes not as a story he tells himself but as a sensory storm—the texture of the belt against his skin, the darkness pressing in, the helplessness. When the memory returns, he feels so overwhelmed by the emotion that he has to stop whatever he is doing. He has called his sister from the parking lot at work, unable to speak, unable to explain. He has sat on the bathroom floor of his apartment for an hour, simply breathing, waiting for his body to believe it is safe. These episodes are so consuming that Marcus has begun to withdraw from the few relationships he has. He has started making excuses not to see his sister, not to attend his cousin's birthday dinner. The safer choice, he has come to believe, is to be alone—not because he wants solitude, but because he cannot bear the thought of being vulnerable in front of another person. He is certain that if anyone really looked at him, they would see what happened, would see the damage written across him like a scar. He feels like an object, something broken and marked, not like a person anymore.

This sense of being exposed, of carrying his trauma visibly, feeds back into his vigilance. When Marcus is around other people—his coworkers, his neighbors, anyone—he monitors their faces for signs of judgment or disgust. He watches for the moment when they might see him as he sees himself. A child crying in a hallway at the hotel triggers the same fear his stepfather's voice once did; it is not just the sound but what it means, the reminder that harm happens in the dark, in enclosed spaces, behind closed doors where no one can help. He avoids the residential floors when possible, takes a different route through the service corridors. He has become so consumed by the need to prevent harm—to himself, to others—that he is slowly withdrawing from his job, from his life. His supervisor has begun to ask questions. Marcus knows he cannot keep this up. The avoidance that once felt like survival is now suffocating him. He came to his first therapy appointment exhausted, afraid, and desperate for the nighttime to stop being a place where he has to choose between reliving trauma and destroying his own rest.
